The D.C. Circuit, in trying to carry forward the principle of Paralyzed 
Veterans^ has at times invoked Hoctor^ albeit reiterating the opinion’s caveat 
that not every numerical rule is legislative. See, e.g., Catholic Health 
Initiatives v, Sebelius, 617 F.3d 490, 495—96 (D.C. Cir. 2010). More broadly, 
the D.C. Circuit tends to identify a rule as legislative the more it perceives the 
rule to differ in specificity from the preexisting norm (statute or prior 
legislative rule) that it purports to construe. See, e.g., Electronic Privacy Info. 
Center v. U.S. Dep’t of Homeland Security, 653 F.3d 1, 7 (D.C. Cir. 2011) 
(contrasting the Transportation Security Administration’s general statutory 
mandate to “develop and test advanced screening technology” with its specific 
deployment of advanced imaging technology scanners to produce nude images 
of passengers). And yet an increase in specificity is not, itself, supposed to be 
enough to render a rule legislative. See Central Texas Telephone Cooperative, 
Inc. V. FCC, 402 F.3d 205, 214 (D.C. Cir. 2005) (“[A]n agency may [lawfully] 
use an interpretative rule to transform ‘a vague statutory duty or right into a 
sharply delineated duty or right.’ ”).
In Paralyzed Veterans, the D.C. Circuit not only suggested that a rule’s 
interpretive status rested on the determinacy with which it flowed from the 
preexisting statute or legislative rule, but also that an interpretive rule 
(when derived from a preexisting legislative rule) could never be changed 
unless the agency altered the preexisting legislative rule as well, which 
would require notice and comment. “Once an agency gives its [legislative] 
regulation an interpretation,” said the court, “it can only change that as it 
would formally modify the regulation itself: through the process of notice 
and comment rulemaking.” 117 F.3d at 586. This principle arguably follows 
from Paralyzed Veterans' larger concept of interpretive rules: If a rule, in 
order to be interpretive, must be determinately derived from a preexisting 
norm, then changing the rule ought to arouse suspicion. If the derivation
